video_title: Cake Wallet Founder Vik Sharma: Why We Forked Signal to Add Bitcoin Payments
gist: Cake Wallet founder Vik Sharma explains Radar Chat, a Signal fork that adds self-custodial Bitcoin/Lightning payments while staying interoperable with Signal, then ranges across Bitcoin wallet security (Coldcard hack, OpenSats-funded red team), the risk of restricting US access to Chinese open AI models, a detailed steel-tariff economics case study from his family's steel business, and a debt-driven Bitcoin macro thesis, closing with tax strategy (Roth IRA) and price/adoption predictions.

themes.theme: Radar Chat: forking Signal to add Bitcoin payments

insights.claim: Radar Chat is a fork of Signal that keeps the same server backend so it remains message-compatible with unmodified Signal, letting Radar users message Signal contacts (and vice versa) with neither side needing to switch apps or even notice a difference.
insights.speaker: Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: A compatibility-first wedge strategy lowers the switching cost for Bitcoin payment adoption versus asking users to migrate to an entirely new messaging network.
insights.quote: Radar and Signal can communicate with each other.

insights.claim: Radar's Bitcoin/Lightning payment feature was made feasible by Spark's Lightning implementation, which Sharma's team used to bolt self-custodial Bitcoin payments onto the forked Signal codebase.
insights.speaker: Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: Signals that Spark-based Lightning tooling is becoming an enabling layer for other apps to add Bitcoin payments quickly, worth tracking as an infrastructure play.

insights.claim: Radar is live on both Android and iOS, uses the same Signal login credentials, and users can restore a Signal cloud backup directly into Radar to migrate all existing messages with no visible change to contacts.
insights.speaker: Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: Zero-friction onboarding via existing Signal backups is a concrete distribution advantage that could accelerate real-world adoption faster than a cold-start messaging app.
insights.quote: None of your friends and family are going to know you're using another app.

insights.claim: Radar already supports point-of-sale spending: a user can pay in person at a merchant's Square terminal today if the merchant has enabled Bitcoin/Lightning acceptance.
insights.speaker: Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: Real-world point-of-sale interoperability with existing payment terminals (not just peer-to-peer) is a leading indicator of Bitcoin's usability as day-to-day money.
insights.quote: You can walk in Radar where somebody takes that Square terminal if they have the Bitcoin payment feature turned on. You can pay with Radar right now.

insights.claim: Sharma's inspiration for merging messaging and payments came from watching his Chinese suppliers pay via WeChat during roughly 50 business trips to China for his steel company, years before Apple Pay existed.
insights.speaker: Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: WeChat's super-app messaging-plus-payments model is a proven, decade-old template that Western Bitcoin apps are now explicitly trying to replicate with self-custody instead of a centralized ledger.

insights.claim: Despite personally disliking stablecoins, Sharma plans to add a stablecoin-denominated (USD-equivalent) balance view and fiat on/off-ramps to bank accounts and debit cards in Radar, because mainstream users are uncomfortable seeing a fluctuating Bitcoin balance and stablecoins act as a low-friction gateway into Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: Even a Bitcoin-maximalist-leaning founder is building stablecoin rails as a UX necessity, evidence that stablecoins will likely remain the dominant onboarding layer for retail crypto payments regardless of ideological preference.
insights.quote: The fact that stable coins are backed by the system that Bitcoin was supposed to protect you against and then going back to that seems kind of silly, but it's a good gateway for people to start using cryptocurrency.

themes.theme: Cake Wallet origins and self-custody philosophy

insights.claim: Cake Wallet was born in 2016 after Coinbase froze Sharma's account within seconds of him sending Bitcoin directly from Coinbase to the Alphabay darknet market, exposing him to custodial-platform chain-analysis surveillance and pushing him toward self-custody.
insights.speaker: Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: A concrete, dated example of exchange-level chain analysis and account freezing in action, illustrating custodial counterparty risk that self-custody wallets are built to solve.
insights.quote: I sent Bitcoin directly from my Coinbase account like a fool... within seconds I got an email like, I mean I pressed enter and boom got an email. You violated your terms, please move your funds.

insights.claim: Cake Wallet's core design philosophy was deliberate radical simplicity, minimizing the number of clicks and options a user faces, which Sharma credits for rapid early adoption of a self-custody product among non-technical users.
insights.speaker: Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: UX simplicity, not just security features, is presented as the key growth lever for self-custody wallet adoption among mainstream (non-crypto-native) users.
insights.quote: Cake wallet is for noobs by noobs because I just wanted it to be very easy.

insights.claim: Sharma began Bitcoin mining in late 2013 with ASIC miners bought on eBay, producing about 0.2 BTC per day, worth roughly $40/day at the time versus a far higher dollar value today.
insights.speaker: Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: Illustrates how retail/hobbyist ASIC mining economics from 2013 have been completely displaced by industrial-scale mining, useful context for valuing long-dated small miner holdings.

themes.theme: Bitcoin wallet security: Coldcard hack, open-source complacency, and quantum risk

insights.claim: The Coldcard hack exposed a systemic complacency in Bitcoin open source software: the community broadly 'cheers for open source' but individuals and companies rarely audit the code themselves, assuming someone smarter has already reviewed it.
insights.speaker: Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: A structural governance gap in Bitcoin infrastructure security — investors and users should not assume 'open source' alone implies adequate security auditing of wallets they hold funds in.
insights.quote: We always cheer for open source, yet there's all this open-source code out there that nobody's reviewing. We think somebody else is doing it.

insights.claim: Sharma donated $10,000 to OpenSats on the day of the Coldcard hack disclosure to fund a volunteer 'red team' auditing Bitcoin wallet software, and that same red team subsequently found and privately disclosed vulnerabilities in Cake Wallet, which were fixed.
insights.speaker: Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: A live example of the Bitcoin ecosystem funding independent security auditing after a major incident; the red team's ongoing work is a signal worth monitoring for future wallet vulnerability disclosures.

insights.claim: Security researchers behind the OpenSats-funded red-team effort, via the Bitcoin Policy Institute, have petitioned the White House to loosen restrictions on advanced AI model access for security auditing, arguing that if Chinese frontier models remain the most capable open tools, the US falls behind in a way that constitutes a national security risk.
insights.speaker: host framing, confirmed by Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: Bitcoin security research is now directly entangled with US AI policy; restrictive AI access rules could indirectly weaken Bitcoin ecosystem security auditing capacity.

insights.claim: Sharma's framework for the long-term quantum computing threat to Bitcoin is that defenders must continuously build stronger cryptographic defenses rather than trying to contain or ban the underlying technology, and that quantum-resistant encryption proposals already exist and could be implemented into Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: Suggests quantum resistance will likely arrive as a protocol upgrade path rather than an existential unsolved risk, relevant for long-horizon Bitcoin holders worried about quantum FUD.
insights.quote: We just have to keep building a bigger monster to fight the bigger monster we've created.

themes.theme: AI policy, China, and open models

insights.claim: Sharma calls US moves to regulate/restrict advanced AI model access 'a huge blunder,' comparing it unfavorably to the early-1990s FCC's hands-off, wait-and-see approach to internet regulation, and warns that restricting domestic access mainly cedes ground to Chinese AI competitors.
insights.speaker: Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: A builder-level view that AI regulatory overreach is a competitiveness risk versus China, relevant to how investors should read US AI policy debates and their effect on US AI companies' relative position.
insights.quote: This would be the first time where the US government has tried to regulate something so early... I think it's a huge blunder by the administration.

insights.claim: Cake Wallet has shifted internal workflows to use Chinese AI models (Kimi, DeepSeek) but avoids routing data directly to the Chinese companies' own servers, instead using third-party hosts like OpenRouter that run the same models on non-Chinese infrastructure to sidestep data-sovereignty concerns.
insights.speaker: Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: A working pattern for Western companies to capture the capability/cost benefits of leading Chinese open models while managing data-residency risk — a template other firms may replicate.

insights.claim: Cake Wallet is building its own GPU compute cluster using Nvidia hardware, indicating the company is investing directly in AI infrastructure rather than relying solely on third-party AI APIs.
insights.speaker: Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: Even a mid-sized crypto wallet company is now capitalizing its own AI compute, a small data point on broader enterprise Nvidia GPU demand outside hyperscalers.

themes.theme: Steel industry tariff economics as a real-world case study

insights.claim: Contrary to the narrative that the US no longer produces steel, US output has only declined from an all-time record of 120 million tons in 1974 to about 80 million tons today, while China now produces over one billion tons annually — more than 10x the US and far ahead of Japan's roughly 110 million tons.
insights.speaker: Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: Corrects a common macro talking point; useful baseline data for anyone analyzing US industrial capacity, reshoring narratives, or steel/metals equities.
insights.quote: China produces over a billion tons of steel. I mean, it's mindboggling. No one in the history of the world has ever done that.

insights.claim: Steel tariffs work opposite to typical tariff effects: instead of raising domestic material costs, they lowered the price of scrap steel (the main US feedstock) because tariffs cut off foreign converters in countries like Turkey and Mexico from importing US scrap, processing it cheaply, and re-exporting finished steel back to the US, removing scrap dealers' export leverage over domestic mills.
insights.speaker: Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: A non-obvious tariff transmission mechanism specific to steel: tariffs can compress input costs even as they protect output prices, directly widening domestic producer margins — a nuance generalist macro takes on tariffs usually miss.
insights.quote: Weirdly in the steel industry it's the raw material becomes cheaper which is scrap... your profit increases actually in the steel industry, whereas in everything else the price of the raw material goes up.

insights.claim: The combination of falling scrap input costs and tariff-protected output prices widened domestic steelmaker margins so much that Sharma directly attributes it to Nucor and US Steel posting roughly $23 billion in profit in a single year.
insights.speaker: Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: Quantifies the tariff-driven margin windfall for major US steel producers, directly relevant to valuing steel equities under continued tariff policy.
insights.quote: So that's why you're seeing companies like New Core and US Steel make you know 23 billion dollars in profit in one year because of that phenomenon.

insights.claim: Sharma argues tariffs and protectionism are only a 'very short-term fix' that 'dampens innovation,' contrasting this with the 1970s-80s wave of US steel mill automation (rolling mill speeds rising roughly 10-20x, from ~100 meters/min to 1,000-2,000 meters/min) that let the industry consolidate and stay competitive without protection.
insights.speaker: Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: A builder-turned-policy-skeptic view that protection removes the competitive pressure needed to drive real productivity gains, relevant to evaluating whether current tariff-driven profit windfalls will translate into durable competitiveness or complacency.

themes.theme: Debt, dollar debasement, and the Bitcoin macro thesis

insights.claim: Sharma believes the US has 'crossed a point of no return' on debt after recently surpassing $40 trillion, implying continued money-printing is now structurally unavoidable regardless of which political party holds office, citing a River chart showing both parties have expanded debt similarly across cycles.
insights.speaker: Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: Reinforces a bipartisan-debasement thesis often used to justify long-term hard-asset allocation; the cited River debt-by-party chart is a concrete reference point to look up.
insights.quote: I mean, it seems like we've crossed a point of no return. Let's see what happens now. And I think that's where Bitcoin plays a huge part.

insights.claim: The stock market and tax receipts now effectively 'back' the US dollar, meaning policymakers cannot allow equities or tax receipts to fall materially without resorting to the money printer, which structurally constrains Fed and Treasury policy choices under Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
insights.speaker: Natalie Brunell (framing endorsed by Vik Sharma)
insights.so_what: A lens for interpreting Fed/Treasury behavior: expect policy to lean toward supporting asset prices and tax receipts even at the cost of further currency debasement, favoring hard-asset hedges.
insights.quote: The stocks kind of back up the US dollar at this point. They can't afford to have tax receipts decrease. They can't afford to have the stock market shake.

insights.claim: Sharma frames Bitcoin's core purpose as direct protection of individuals from currency debasement by centralized monetary authorities, tying it explicitly to the $40 trillion debt milestone.
insights.speaker: Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: Reaffirms the debasement-hedge thesis as the guest's primary lens for Bitcoin's value proposition, independent of short-term price action.
insights.quote: That's why Bitcoin is invented, right? To protect the common person from that, from a centralized manipulator.

themes.theme: Bitcoin price predictions, volatility, and tax strategy

insights.claim: Sharma publicly walks back his earlier prediction that Bitcoin would reach $800,000, admitting it has not materialized despite spot ETF approval and corporate treasury buying (e.g., Michael Saylor's purchases), and says he has 'stopped making that prediction.'
insights.speaker: Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: A credible insider's admission that ETF inflows and corporate treasury demand have not been sufficient by themselves to hit aggressive price targets, tempering overly bullish near-term price narratives.
insights.quote: I thought we'd be at 800,000 by now, which I'm surprised we're not.

insights.claim: Sharma now argues that declining volatility, not price level, is the more meaningful and already-achieved Bitcoin milestone: he says Bitcoin's realized volatility has steadily fallen over its roughly 17-18 year history and may now be comparable to or lower than gold's, even though gold has a 5,000-year track record.
insights.speaker: Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: Reframes the bull case away from price targets toward a volatility-compression thesis, which is a more falsifiable and arguably more institutionally relevant metric for portfolio allocation decisions.
insights.quote: Bitcoin, the price is the loudest fact about Bitcoin, but it's the least profound.

insights.claim: Sharma's five-year vision for Bitcoin adoption centers on a regulatory change exempting small transactions (he floats thresholds like $250-$500) from capital gains tax, so Bitcoin can be spent on everyday purchases like coffee without triggering a taxable event.
insights.speaker: Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: A concrete, trackable policy ask (de minimis crypto tax exemption) that, if enacted, would materially increase Bitcoin's usability as everyday money and is worth monitoring in US tax legislation.
insights.quote: Even if it's something small, even if we start out with $500, $250, start somewhere so you can walk in and use radar chat and pay for coffee.

insights.claim: Sharma's argument for holding Bitcoin in a Roth IRA is tax optimization: eventual liquidation of Bitcoin into depreciating fiat currency is a taxable event outside a Roth, whereas gains inside a Roth (his example: turning $5,000 into $500,000) can be withdrawn entirely tax-free.
insights.speaker: Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: A concrete, actionable tax-structuring point for individual Bitcoin investors: using a Roth wrapper can eliminate capital gains tax on long-term Bitcoin appreciation at withdrawal.
insights.quote: If you do it in a Roth, you could turn $5,000 into a half million and you're going to take it all out entirely taxfree.

insights.claim: Sharma wants to see more real-world Bitcoin usage as actual money for goods and services rather than just as a speculative asset, noting that when he tweeted 'Bitcoin should be used as money' a couple years ago he was attacked even by pro-Bitcoin VC firms, illustrating internal ecosystem disagreement over Bitcoin's primary use case.
insights.speaker: Vik Sharma
insights.so_what: Highlights an unresolved ideological split within the Bitcoin investor/VC community between 'store of value only' and 'medium of exchange' camps, relevant to which infrastructure (like Radar/Lightning apps) gets funded and adopted going forward.
insights.quote: A couple years ago I tweeted about Bitcoin should be used as money and people jumped all over me. Even like big VC firms.
